Variety reports the "Barbie" sequel is hitting roadblocks.

The issue? The head of Warner Bros. is refusing to meet the salary demands of Greta Gerwig, Ryan Gosling, and Margot Robbie.

Over the past three years, the studio has made six separate offers—all rejected. The latest, pitched this spring, was reportedly historic in scale.

While the cast's asks are undeniably high, the studio is prepared to make major concessions. The main obstacle? WB boss David Zaslav, who insists Gerwig and her team aren't worth the price tag.

Adding pressure: a tight deadline. Production must begin by December, or the project collapses. If that happens, rights revert to Mattel, who could take the film elsewhere—ushering in an entirely new creative team.

📌 Browser Extensions: Why a Chrome Wallet Is Its Own Risk Layer

Main Points
⏺ A browser wallet lives in the same environment as sites, scripts, and other extensions
⏺ Browser or website attacks can push users into dangerous signatures
⏺ This post explains why wallet convenience needs discipline

1️⃣ Core Idea — extensions make dApp access easy, but they place your wallet inside the browser flow.
2️⃣ Attack Surface — phishing sites, fake popups, malicious extensions, and swapped links.
3️⃣ Common Mistake — users recognize the interface and sign without reading the action.
4️⃣ Separation — use a dedicated browser/profile for crypto instead of mixing it with daily browsing.
5️⃣ Practical Hygiene — keep extensions minimal, use bookmarks, verify domains, and simulate large transactions.

Final Thoughts

Browser wallets are convenient, but they live in a noisy environment. The more clutter around them, the higher the chance of signing the wrong thing.

⚖️ Minnesota bans crypto ATMs after $1M in scam losses

Minnesota has enacted a law banning crypto ATMs statewide, effective this past Saturday, eliminating a category of machines previously used by residents to purchase Bitcoin and other digital assets.

State officials linked approximately $1 million in scam-related losses to crypto kiosks between 2023 and 2025, with senior citizens identified as the primary victims. The ban follows a broader trend of U.S. states scrutinizing crypto ATM operators over fraud exposure, particularly targeting elderly users who may be more vulnerable to social engineering schemes involving kiosk-based transfers.

➡️ Crypto crime has moved beyond online hacks, Chainalysis says 

🌐 Chainalysis has warned that cryptocurrency crime has increasingly extended into kidnappings, home invasions and other violent incidents as criminals pursue holders who can transfer digital assets immediately under coercion. According to the blockchain analytics firm’s latest report shared with cryptonews, cybercrime still accounts for most illicit crypto activity, including an estimated $3.4 billion stolen through hacks, $17 billion lost to scams and about $820 million linked to ransomware in 2025. 

⭐️ At the same time, physical attacks have become more common because crypto holders often control large amounts of wealth through self-custody wallets without the institutional safeguards associated with traditional financial assets. 

📊 The report estimates that violent criminals have extracted more than $30 million from crypto holders during the first half of 2026 through successful kidnappings, hostage situations, and home invasions. If the current pace continues, 2026 would surpass the $58 million stolen during 2025, although the estimate only covers publicly reported incidents and likely understates the full scale of the problem.

Syria: Who Funds, Who Threatens, Who Drills

Iranian media claim Tehran has warned Ankara, Baghdad, Doha and Riyadh that any Syrian military operation in Lebanon would trigger a regional conflict — with Iran threatening strikes on more than 100 strategic sites inside Syria, including the presidential palace.

The alleged scenario is schematic enough to run as a Pentagon simulation: Syrian forces enter Lebanon, declare Tripoli a zone of influence, pressure Hezbollah’s missile infrastructure in the Bekaa Valley, and force a new security arrangement. 

Iran’s answer, according to the reports, is that Syria would not be entering Lebanon. It would be entering a wider war.

The financing map is even more revealing. The UAE is reported to be willing to fund Syrian troops and operations. Qatar is said to oppose the plan. Saudi Arabia allegedly has no objection, provided Hezbollah is weakened without setting the region on fire.

A regional coalition, in other words, is being assembled around the least workable business model: pay someone else’s army to dismantle someone else’s militia in someone else’s country, without starting a war that ruins the investment.

Damascus has repeatedly denied plans to intervene in Lebanon. Syrian officials have said their goal is to prevent escalation, not export it. 

Analysts have also questioned whether Syria has the military capacity to confront Hezbollah directly; the more realistic Syrian role would be disrupting smuggling routes from Iraq through Syria into Lebanon.

Hezbollah sees the issue differently. It treats any Syrian move not as an independent Damascus decision, but as part of an American-Israeli project to break the “resistance” network from the east after Israel failed to impose a decisive outcome in the south.

Then, quietly, another American project begins.

A U.S. oil company has reportedly sent seismic survey trucks into Syria’s Hasakah province. The vehicles send vibrations into the ground, mapping geological layers before drilling for oil and gas. No ideology is required. Just data, contracts and a stable security zone.

That may be the most practical regional plan of all. Once American firms start extracting Syrian oil, Washington will want the ground quiet. Keeping it quiet requires an army that can hold it. 

And a Syrian army built under U.S. protection will need Hezbollah, Iran, Turkey, Gulf money and local militias to stop interfering with the business plan.

The Middle East’s newest peace formula is not a treaty.

It is a drilling permit.
